AIR QUALITY · INDIA · 2020–2025

Seventy-two months of air,
487 stations.

An exploration of PM2.5, PM10, NO2, SO2, CO, NH3 and ozone across 31 states and union territories: averages, station look-ups, missing values, regions and seasons, and trends.

Please read: this dataset is synthetic. Every one of the 245,448 rows in the source file carries the label “SYNTHETIC - NOT HISTORICAL OBSERVATIONS”. Everything below is a faithful analysis of that file, but it describes generated data, so none of it should be read as real measurements of Indian air.
DATA OVERVIEW & QUALITY

What is in the file

One row per station, pollutant and month (1st of each month, Jan 2020 to Dec 2025). The panel is perfectly balanced: 487 stations × 7 pollutants × 72 months.

Checks that passed

    Quirks you should know about

      These filters drive Q1, Q3, Q4 and Q5. Q2 has its own station picker.
      QUESTION 1

      Average particulate matter concentration

      Mean of the monthly station averages for PM2.5 and PM10 (µg/m³). Missing readings are excluded unless the median-fill box is ticked. Reference limits are India’s NAAQS: annual 40 / 60 and 24-hour 60 / 100 for PM2.5 / PM10. Because this file holds monthly averages, the annual limit is the fairer yardstick.

      QUESTION 2

      Filter by monitoring station and date range

      Pick a station and a month range to see its readings. Missing months are shown as such.

      QUESTION 3

      Handling missing pollutant values

      Each pollutant’s missing share, and the median used to fill gaps when the box above is ticked. Medians are computed per pollutant across all valid readings, so pollutants are never mixed. Filling with one median is simple but flattens variation, which is why it is optional.

      Stations with the most missing data

      QUESTION 4

      Group by region and season

      Winter = Dec–Feb, Summer = Mar–May, Monsoon = Jun–Sep, Post-Monsoon = Oct–Nov, as labelled in the file.

      QUESTION 5

      Trends in pollutant levels

      The monthly national average over time, plus the ten highest states. Watch the yearly row: the levels repeat from year to year, so the pattern is seasonal rather than a long-term rise or fall.

      FINDINGS

      What the data says

        Source: India_Air_Quality_2020_2025.csv (245,448 rows, synthetic). Reference limits: CPCB NAAQS (2009). All figures are computed in your browser from the embedded data.
